text: Tesla Adds GTA-Like Update to FSD # ‘It’s Like GTA’: Musk Touts Video Game-Like Update to Tesla FSD FSD v15 was released to some vehicles on Saturday. Its visualization system may be the most remarkable part. By Mike Pearl Published November 21, 2026, 5:53 pm ET ![Tesla Fsd Gta](https://gizmodo.com/app/uploads/2026/11/tesla-fsd-gta.jpg) © Tesla on X / Gizmodo screenshot Tesla announced an update on Saturday to its Full Self-Driving (Supervised) software platform, also known as FSD. The release notes for the update, FSD v15, include a long list of apparent safety and performance improvements. The most intriguing piece of the update, however, is a video game-like flourish called Tesla Reality View, which renders a moveable, photorealistic, full-motion view of your car’s surroundings from an imaginary virtual camera situated just above and behind you, sort of like the Lakitu Bros. in Super Mario 64. > FSD v15 now starting to roll out – upgrading every part of the end-to-end driving network > > Safety 25x better handling of safety critical cases > > Tesla Reality View Adds a live visualization of the drive that lets you see & control what FSD is planning to do > > Navigation for start… pic.twitter.com/Sfjk4wZecW > > — Tesla (@Tesla) November 21, 2026 But that’s not the video game that came to mind for Elon Musk when he posted on X about the feature: > It’s like GTA https://t.co/H2H9tjTStt > > — Elon Musk (@elonmusk) November 21, 2026 “It’s like GTA,” Musk wrote. And with GTA VI raking in billions of dollars over the past few days, who can blame Musk for piggybacking on the zeitgeist? The release notes say Tesla Reality View “ lets you see & control what FSD is planning to do.” The third-person perspective it provides is essentially the same as the trailing view provided by previous versions of the feature, but instead of displaying a rendering of your car on the road, along with a few key features in an otherwise empty and mostly colorless dreamscape, it renders the whole world around your car. Intuitively, being able to see everything going on around you in a familiar, game-like way does seem like it might (might) be easier to comprehend and comforting to use. In a way, it’s the ultimate fulfillment of the 2001-era dream of the character in the original the Fast and the Furious who plays the racing game Gran Turismo on a Playstation wired to the infotainment system in his car while waiting for a real-life race to start. It’s worth noting that he’s using the Tesla Reality View-like trailing camera mode in Gran Turismo, as most normal people do. But one can’t help but think disquieting thoughts about what happens when the guy with the controller in his hands stops comprehending any difference at all between the video game world on his screen and the real world of metal, concrete, flesh, and blood on the other side of his windshield. As for the rest of the changes, Fred Lambert at Electrek writes that the list of upgrades “reads like a list of FSD’s biggest current weaknesses.” It’s supposed to have fewer problems around potholes, school zones, speed cameras, standing water, and more. But Lambert also writes that “FSD has never improved in a straight line,” and says, “Every major version has brought real gains along with new problems, and point releases regularly go backward.”
